title: Browser AI Speedup: 200+ GPU Kernels Generated on the Fly, Not Precompiled
dek: In-browser AI has no 'universally optimal kernel': a kernel is the implementation of an operator on a specific piece of hardware, and different devices have different optima. The 200+ kernels are not hardcoded programs but templates that are generated in the browser for your device.
why: An 11-minute solo release demo, no back-and-forth, medium density. The point that kernels must be tailored to the device is made clearly; the templated kernels and Fleet's crowdsourced tuning mechanism are worth a close look.
who: Engineers running LLMs in the browser or building high-performance front-end AI applications, and technical decision-makers interested in WebGPU and WASM local inference solutions.
skip: The code walkthrough in the opening demo and the release channel introduction at the end can be sped up; focus on the kernel templating mechanism and the Fleet data feedback section.

points.h: Operators define, kernels run on hardware
points.body: The transcript first distinguishes two concepts: a model is a large graph of operators, and an operator is just a mathematical definition—addition is A+B. A kernel is the implementation that brings that definition to specific hardware. The same add, in the browser, goes through WebGPU/WGSL; in other ecosystems it corresponds to a CUDA or Metal kernel. The two are often conflated, but the speed difference comes precisely from the latter: if the underlying kernel is fast, the whole inference graph can be fast. This also explains why it's worth polishing a kernel for a simple operation repeatedly, rather than vaguely tuning a 'general math library'.

points.h: What's released is Jinja templates, not hardcoded kernels
points.body: The difference in approach is worth noting: the repo doesn't contain hardcoded WGSL files one by one, but several Jinja templates that use if/else to describe branches for different devices. At execution time, the library validates the template, selects the appropriate data type and workgroup size, and renders it into the WGSL most suitable for the current GPU adapter to run. For example, in the same addition function, the left side has a narrow data type and small workgroup size; the right side, because the device supports wider data types and larger workgroups, runs faster even though it's the same add. The official release lists 200+ kernel entries, but what's actually delivered is the ability to 'make kernels on the fly for the hardware'.

points.h: Attention mechanism in the browser takes only about 20 lines of JS
points.body: The demo brings abstraction back to reality: running a small attention mechanism in the browser required only about 20 lines of JavaScript. The flow is text → token → vector, but a token's vector can't be viewed in isolation; you have to see how other tokens in the context affect it. The code just loads four kernels from the Hub—matmul, softmax, add, layer normalization—and the rest of the scheduling and GPU data exchange is hidden by the Hugging Face Kernels library. The heavy lifting is all at the kernel layer, which is why the barrier to 'local inference in the browser' has dropped.

points.h: The entire wave animation is just one matrix multiplication
points.body: The same demo gives an intuitive comparison: 128 waves pass through a 1024×1024 matrix, and each cell's color is an RGBA computed by a matrix multiplication. The animation of over a million pixels runs at about 60fps under WebGPU—60 is not the compute limit, just requestAnimationFrame locking rendering to 60; the kernel itself can compute at about 400fps. Running the same logic in plain JavaScript yields roughly 6.75fps. The gap isn't in the math, but in whether someone has written it as an implementation that hugs this particular GPU—that's what those kernels do.

points.h: Fleet turns user devices into tuning data via testing
points.body: Fleet is ostensibly a benchmark page: anyone can run their own GPU and see how it performs in comparison. But the project team says it plainly: the team only has a few devices of their own, while the real world has thousands of WebGPU devices, possibly with edge cases they haven't thought of—some kernels might perform poorly on your machine, or even fail outright. Fleet collects runtime data from real devices to continue optimization, and the improved kernels, being open source, return to all users. When you click 'Run Benchmark', you're not just seeing a score; you're also doing a round of real-environment adaptation testing for the project.

terms.def: The implementation of an operator on specific hardware; the same addition needs different kernels on different GPUs.
WebGPU Shading Language, the language for writing kernels in the WebGPU environment; it's the bridge to the GPU in the browser.
A Python template engine; Hugging Face uses .jinja files to describe kernels, then renders them into WGSL at runtime based on the device.
The next-generation API for accessing the GPU from the browser; the computational foundation for local AI inference on the browser side.
